messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 23
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Urban Planner
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Object Throwing: Throwing objects, Expressions of Anger: Other people expressing anger, even calmly, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong, Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement, Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
  Threat: Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
  Memory: Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down, Low Coping: I can't deal with even the slightest upset, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kwame is a 23-year-old urban planner who came to treatment after months of feeling as if ordinary city life had become charged with danger. The assault happened late one evening after he left a neighborhood meeting where residents had argued heatedly about a redevelopment proposal. In the parking lot, a man who had been drinking confronted him, accused him of disrespect, and began shouting. Kwame remembers the smell of alcohol first, then a bottle hurled past him, then the man’s face tightening with anger as another object came toward him. What stays with him is not a smooth story but a set of pictures: the flash of the bottle leaving the man’s hand, the look on his face, the sharp movement in the corner of Kwame’s vision. When he tries to say more, he stalls out. He says he knows what happened, but the words disappear, and if he pushes himself he becomes so overwhelmed that he has to stop talking.

In the weeks afterward, those few frozen images seemed to attach themselves to parts of the world around him. At work, when a colleague tossed a set of rolled plans onto a table, his body jerked before he knew why. On site visits, if two residents started arguing, even in controlled voices, he felt a surge of alarm as though anger itself meant something violent was about to happen. Passing someone on the train who smelled of alcohol could make the parking lot scene feel abruptly near again. Because the memory was stored for him as sensory fragments rather than something he could place firmly in the past, the city kept presenting moments that felt like pieces of the assault returning. Those moments did not only remind him; they made him feel sure that the people and systems meant to keep order had failed him once and would fail him again, and that if danger started he would be unable to stop it.

As these reminders accumulated, Kwame became convinced that safety was not something he could trust. Friends telling him he was fine did not land. He startled at ordinary sounds in the office, and sudden movement beside him on crowded sidewalks made him flinch hard enough to step back or raise an arm defensively. Once he was in that keyed-up state, the next thrown object, the next irritated voice, the next trace of alcohol registered instantly. He had come to believe that he could not handle even minor upset anymore, so any sign of tension felt like proof that something was about to go badly and that he would be helpless in it.

He began organizing his life around not feeling that jolt. In meetings he worked hard to smooth over disagreement before it developed, and if discussion sharpened he would withdraw, let others decide, or leave the room on the pretext of a call. He started avoiding residents and coworkers he knew were blunt or easily frustrated. After work he sometimes went to casinos, telling himself the noise and bright focus gave him somewhere else to put his mind; at other times he would lie awake replaying what he had done wrong in the parking lot, dwelling on whether he should have left earlier, answered differently, seen it coming. The reminders drove these habits, but the habits deepened the problem. The more he backed away from conflict and chased distraction, the less capable he felt, and the more he blamed himself for becoming someone who could not manage ordinary friction.

Those patterns also fed the assault back into the center of his mind. Nights after gambling, or after an afternoon spent mentally picking apart his own mistakes, the memory returned in the same blinding snapshots, with the same inability to put it into words. Avoiding disagreement at work meant that even mild irritation in other people remained untested and ominous, so expressions of anger became more potent triggers, not less. His constant scanning for movement and sound kept him physically braced, and when he startled, the body reaction pulled the images back with it: bottle, face, motion. In turn, each return of the memory seemed to confirm what he now feared about himself and the world—that protection cannot be relied on, that bad things happen without warning, and that he will not be able to cope.

The consequences have become concrete in his job. Urban planning had suited him because he liked negotiation and public process; now he avoids the very meetings that are central to his role, and his supervisor has noticed that he passes contentious community sessions to coworkers. He is still single and says he has kept more to himself, partly because he cannot explain what happened without shutting down and partly because he does not trust feeling safe with other people. He finally sought help after a coworker, speaking sharply but not aggressively, slapped a folder onto a conference table and Kwame recoiled so visibly that the room went silent. What frightened him most was not only the reaction itself, but the certainty that his world was shrinking around these moments. What he hopes for, cautiously, is to be able to walk into work and into the city without every angry tone, thrown object, stray smell of alcohol, or sudden movement feeling like the assault is happening again.
